description: Too weird for Earth, too grounded for space. We turn NASA data into ideas that land. 🛸
summary:
We built Bezra (Arabic for "seed") because a farmer gets one try a year, and the climate is changing the rules under his feet.

Bezra lets farmers try their season before they plant it. A farmer draws his field on a map. Bezra pulls NASA data for that exact field: POWER weather, HLS greenness, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS, ECOSTRESS and GPM rainfall. From it we compute crop stage, root-zone water, heat risk and disease risk. A 3D simulator then grows the crop on the field's real satellite image. The farmer changes the sowing date, variety or watering, picks a hot year, and watches the outcome before risking anything real.

After he plants, Bezra gives him one to three clear tasks a day. Each task says how much of his harvest it protects. Every number shows its NASA source, and a friendly seed guide explains it by text or voice. One extension engineer can watch hundreds of fields ranked by risk.

That is our answer to Field Shift: NASA data turned into field-level decisions any farmer can act on today. As seasons shift, Bezra helps every field shift with them. We start with wheat in Egypt and build for every farmer on Earth.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Bezra (Arabic for “seed”) helps a Nile Delta smallholder explore crop-rotation strategies that keep his soil healthy and his farm resilient to heat and water shortage, using NASA data for his exact field. For his current rotation and at least three alternatives, it shows the next 10 years side by side, with:

  • why the rotation could help;
  • the evidence behind it;
  • its benefits;
  • what we don’t know yet;
  • the risks that need local review.

HOW IT WORKS

  1. The field: the farmer draws his field on a real satellite map (Esri World Imagery). ESA WorldCover and OpenStreetMap mask out roads, houses and canals, so only farmland counts.
  2. Data for that exact field:
    • NASA POWER: daily weather since 1990, plus climatology;
    • NASA MODIS MOD13Q1: normal-year greenness, and the field’s past seasons since 2000 via AppEEARS;
    • NASA HLS v2.0 and ESA Sentinel-2 L2A: greenness at 30 m and 10 m;
    • ESA Sentinel-1: irrigation detection;
    • NASA SMAP L4: root-zone soil moisture;
    • NASA ECOSTRESS: crop surface temperature;
    • NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6: climate projections to 2040;
    • Copernicus DEM GLO-30: slope and low spots;
    • ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0: soil 0–30 cm, with its uncertainty;
    • Open-Meteo: 7-day forecast, and archived past forecasts for the hindcast.
  3. Strategies compared: the farmer’s current rotation (for example wheat then rice), plus wheat then maize, berseem one winter in two, short berseem then cotton, a three-year mix with faba bean, sugar beet, and a salt-tolerant option for salty land. Options that don’t fit his land are hidden with the reason, for example rice not licensed or soil too salty.
  4. Soil memory: each strategy runs year after year for 10 years on the field’s real weather, across six past weather windows plus a 2040 warming case. A Soil Ledger carries what each crop leaves behind into the next:
    • organic carbon (RothC);
    • a relative nitrogen balance;
    • salinity (FAO-29), including drainage water and bare summers;
    • puddled soil after rice;
    • broomrape;
    • cereal after cereal.
  5. Starting point from the field’s real past: rice seasons and bare land seen from space since 2000, plus the farmer’s own memory and soil test. When the two disagree, every strategy is run from both pasts, and the ranking must hold in both.
  6. The comparison card, for each strategy:
    “Ten years in 30 seconds” plays two futures of the same field side by side.
    • water per feddan per year;
    • soil health year by year;
    • years with heat damage, now and with ~2040 warming;
    • soil carbon kept;
    • what holds the soil back, and what breaks the decline;
    • the evidence links, the information gaps, and the risks to check locally.
  7. This season, too: a 3D simulator to test sowing date, variety and watering on the field’s real weather; daily tasks; alerts with satellite proof; and Ask Bezra, a seed character that explains any number by text or Arabic voice.
  8. Engineer view: fields ranked by risk, plan approval, and what a village would save in water and soil carbon if farmers switched rotations, month by month for the canal.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

  • Long-term choices: the Delta’s soil is cropped all year, so the order of crops is the only rest it gets. Bezra makes that choice visible years ahead, before yields fall.
  • Field-level advice: every number shows its source, age and confidence.
  • Reaching farmers: a rotation card can be sent on WhatsApp, heard in Arabic, or printed for the extension agent.
  • Open data: we publish an open “Delta Soil Memory” dataset (CC BY 4.0).
  • Scale: we start with the Delta’s main crops, built to work on any field NASA can see.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

  • Most tools advise on one season. Bezra treats soil as having memory and lets the farmer rehearse ten years on a digital copy of his own field.
  • Satellite history sets where his soil starts.
  • Climate data becomes a simple question: “what happens to my soil if I keep doing this?”

DESIGN AND EXPERIENCE

  • Designer-led: every screen was designed in Figma before it was built, with one visual language across the app.
  • Mobile-first: a bottom navigation bar on phones, big touch targets, and every screen tested at phone width.
  • Arabic first: fully right-to-left with IBM Plex Sans Arabic, plus English, and Arabic voice.
  • Easy to learn: a one-minute guided tour, a friendly seed character, and the crop growing in 3D on the field’s real satellite image.
  • Calm and readable: plain-language cards, one clear status line, and motion that respects “reduce motion”.
  • Reliable: works on weak connections with saved results and an offline mode, and says plainly when live data is waking up.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

  • Low digital literacy: plain words, voice, big buttons, Arabic first with English.
  • Honesty:
    • provenance labels on every number, and “I don’t know” when data is missing;
    • a public validation table that also reports what failed, such as no skill against national wheat yields, and that MODIS at 250 m cannot tell wheat from berseem.
  • Safety: Bezra never gives fertilizer or pesticide amounts. The engineer decides.
  • Reach: cached data, an offline mode, and WhatsApp and voice summaries.

VALIDATION DATA
NASA POWER was checked against ERA5 and a NOAA GHCN-Daily station (Alexandria, 2000–2023). The yield index was checked against FAOSTAT Egypt wheat yields. Heat alerts were scored day by day against forecasts archived before each heat wave.

TOOLS

  • Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Three.js.
  • Data and science engine: Python, FastAPI, rasterio, pystac-client, NumPy, httpx.
  • Database: PostgreSQL (Supabase).
  • AI: Google Gemini with Claude as backup (Ask Bezra); the code was written with Claude Code.
  • Design: Figma.
  • Hosting: Vercel and Render.
  • Data access: NASA Earthdata, AppEEARS, CMR-STAC, Earth Search STAC, NASA NCCS THREDDS.
